slides.title: Influence, Not Just Seniority
bullets: "KOL" is often loosely used in pharma to mean simply an important doctor
The real criterion is measurable influence, not seniority or title alone
A prestigious hospital title does not by itself make someone a KOL
Limited scientific output and peer recognition disqualify a title alone

slides.title: How the Industry Identifies a KOL
bullets: Strong publication record in peer-reviewed journals
Leadership as principal or coordinating investigator on trials
Authorship or committee membership on practice guidelines
Invited speaking roles at major congresses
Leadership positions in professional or scientific societies

slides.title: Influence vs. Mere Prominence
bullets: A mid-career researcher can be a true KOL in a narrow sub-specialty
What matters is whether other clinicians actually cite and follow the work
When a KOL shifts opinion, that shift plausibly moves broader practice
Balanced scientific exchange is a legitimate way evidence reaches that opinion

slides.title: KOLs Differ in Type of Influence
bullets: Influence can center on clinical practice, trial design, or guidelines
It can also center on public visibility or peer education
Effective KOL work means knowing which kind of influence someone has
This module builds that nuance through DOLs, rising stars, and mapping

slides.title: Getting This Right Is Foundational
bullets: Correct identification underpins every other skill in this module
Time spent with the wrong expert is time not spent shaping practice
Reputation and hearsay are not reliable substitutes for real criteria

takeaway.title: A true KOL is defined by measurable influence, not title or seniority
bullets: Publications, trials, guidelines and congress roles are the real markers
Influence type varies across clinical, trial, guideline, or peer education
Correct identification is the foundation for segmentation and engagement
